primitives.verbatim_quote: ## Introduction A significant and acute enhancement of exercise capacity can be induced through a mechanism referred to as postactivation performance enhancement (PAPE) (Blazevich and Babault, 2019).
primitives.assumptions: PAPE is a transient neuro-mechanical phenomenon dependent on prior activation history.

The core operator PAPE is defined as a transient enhancement in athletic performance following a conditioning stimulus. It is modeled as a convolution of activation history and physiological response, where ICA acts as a strong facilitator due to its high-intensity isometric nature. The neuromechanical basis of PAPE is supported by evidence showing that reductions in rectus femoris stiffness predict gains in CMJ height, indicating a mechanical facilitation pathway. Thermal effects are ruled out as primary drivers, since SST changes do not correlate with performance gains. The model assumes that PAPE operates within a bounded regime—specifically, when prior fatigue is minimal. Failure modes include overtraining or excessive fatigue, which negate the PAPE effect. The derived kernel framework allows for probabilistic inference in GSI and enables dynamic state transitions in GSE based on activation and stiffness metrics.
